narrative:
Based on your academic record, the model estimates that you have a 90.9% chance of failing the bar exam on the first attempt. Because the law school saw this as an overwhelming risk, your application was denied.

The strongest reason for this decision comes from your Year 3 class standing. Among students who were accepted, the typical class decile is around 6, meaning they ranked near the middle of their class. Your Year 3 decile of 1 places you near the very bottom, which the model views as a powerful indicator that you are not prepared for bar-level material. This was the single biggest factor tipping the prediction toward failure.

The second most influential factor was your LSAT score. While accepted students average about 37, your score of 25.50 is substantially below both that average and the typical range for successful applicants. The LSAT is designed to measure reasoning skills central to passing the bar, so a score this far below average significantly increased the model’s predicted failure risk.

The third most important factor was your Year 1 class standing. Again, you ranked in the bottom decile, while accepted students tend to be around the middle. This early pattern further reinforced the conclusion that you struggled from the start of your legal education.

In short, all three major signals point in the same direction: low class standing in both your first and third years, plus a weak LSAT score, created a very high predicted chance of failing the bar.

To improve your future application, I strongly recommend retaking the LSAT after dedicated prep to raise your score closer to the school’s average. You should also consider strengthening your academic performance through additional coursework. Reapplying later with a stronger record would give you a far more competitive profile.
